content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper studies the sample-2-sample relationship by analyzing the weight updating process in the supervised learning setting. The study (with name lpNTK) suggests that samples could be roughly categorized into interchangeable/unrelated/contradictory samples by measuring their interactions. In addition to providing theoretical analysis that connects lpNTK with previous works (empirical NTK), the authors empirically connected lpNTK with several ML phenomena including learning difficulty and forgetting. content.title: Response to Reviewer HxBc
content.comment:
Thank you Reviewer HxBc for identifying the novelty and solid contribution of this work. In particular, we appreciate your assessment of the thorough theoretical analyses and experiments.

## Q1: How are the hyperparameters selected?

> “Note that we did not fine-tune any hyperparameters, to make sure that the comparison between different instances of datasets are fair” I think a better/fair selection procedure is to follow the same model selection rules and perform hyperparameter selection, instead of not fine-tuning hyperparameters at all. 

We actually followed the commonly used model selection method, i.e. grid-search the hyperparameters that lead to the best validation performance. We then run all our experiment with the same hyperparameters but difference random seeds. Thanks for proposing this question, we will make our method more clear in the future version.

## Q2: Details about the forgetting events?

> In section 3.3 are the forgetting events formally defined? How are they selected in the experiments?

A formal definition of forgetting events is given in Algorithm 2 in Appendix D.3 of the latest version, specifically line 4. During Experiment 2, we cannot select forgetting events. Instead, we observed the forgetting events happened more than 5,000 times in the first 30 training iterations.

## Q3: Performance of simple benchmarking models in Table 1?

> In Table 1 could lpNTK be benchmarked with other methods? How would a simple benchmarking model perform in this case?

We don’t think there is a specific benchmark for forgetting events. But, we’re happy to introduce more baseline in the future. 

## Q4: Why LeNet-5 on MNIST?

> Why LeNet-5 on MNIST?

We used different model architecture on different benchmarks to show that our lpNTK is able to work on various kinds of model architectures.

## Q5: How could lpNTK contribute to self-supervised learning?

> Do you think the framework can be applied to self-supervised learning (esp contrastive learning), where certain loss function can be viewed as a classification of similarity? Could this framework be used to evaluate how similar/unrelated/different samples could contribute to SSL performance?

We’re also exploring the effectiveness of our methods on SSL. Hopefully, we can add such discussion to the future version. In the meantime, we are also open and happy to have a such discussion with researchers working on SSL.

## Q6: What do the selected or pruned examples look like?

> It might be beneficial and insightful to show some examples that are selected and pruned in Appendix.

Thanks for the suggestions! We agree that example samples from MNIST and CIFAR-10 can help to make the superiority of our method more visual. We are happy to add them in the future version.

content.title: Response to Reviewer 2esP
content.comment:
Thank you for identifying the novelty of this work. Regarding the weakness you mentioned, we respond to them below.

# Q1: Each contribution is not big enough, and the point-to-point correlation is not strong enough

> Specifically, the first contribution I think is quite satisfactory, because this is the starting point of this work. However, for the second and third contribution points, one is to explain some phenomena discovered by predecessors, and the other is an application in a small direction. First of all, the relationship between the two is not very large. Second, although both contributions have their corresponding value. But the addition of the two seems to be too scattered in this work.

In Section 3, we aim to show that our lpNTK can provide a unified view to explain multiple learning phenomena, while the existing quantities are restricted to capture only one of them. One thing we want to emphasise is that all these learning phenomena are closely connected, even though they look unrelated to each other.

# Q2: Lack of baselines in Figure 2

> In Figure 2, I don't think it is enough to just comparing with pNTK to highlight the advantages of lpNTK. Authors are advised to introduce more baselines. In addition, what are the specific advantages of the operation of remove redundant samples?

We are happy to introduce more baselines such as E2LN and GradN in the future.

Regarding the removal of redundant samples, we argue that our method can serve as a potential guideline for collecting informative samples in the future.

# Q3: Does the asymptotic convergence of lpNTK hold during training?

> Theorem 1 demonstrates that lpNTK asymptotically convergence to eNTK at initialization. Is this conclusion holds during gradient descent training?

The asymptotic convergence holds when the width of ANNs approaches infinity, regardless of the training time steps.

# Q4: Any formal/informal theoretical explanations of Section 3.2?

> In section 3.2 you claim that the interactions between samples will be weaker when the dataset size is smaller. Do you have some formal/informal theoretical explanations?

According to our results, the lpNTK between two samples is never exactly $0$, which means that any two samples are related (either positively or negatively). So, it is reasonable to model the whole dataset and a fully connected graph where there is always an edge between two arbitrary nodes. That said, for a dataset of size $N$, the number of edges will be $\frac{1}{2} N^2$. With fewer samples, the connections between samples would decrease quadratically.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper provides a (semi-)principled way to quantify the influence of one training datapoint over another point during the training of a deep network. The paper then uses this quantity to understand existing concepts in deep learning, namely that of (a) example difficulty, (b) forgetting events and (c) the success of data pruning. 

Concretely, here are the contributions:
- The proposed quantity is a scalar called the _labeled pseudoNTK_ (lpNTK). This is based off of the _pseudoNTK_ [Mohamadi and Sutherland '22] but with a key twist that incorporates the target label. 
- The authors intuitively derive how lpNTK arises when one writes down the effect of a parameter update from one point on the prediction at another.
- The authors empirically show that the learning difficulty of an example [in the sense of Jiang et al '2021] correlates well with lpNTK. 
- The authors empirically aruge that learning difficulty is not "inherent" to a point but rather a by-product of inter-sample relationships.
-  The authors empirically demonstrate how lpNTK can also help identify points that are easily forgotten as in Toneva et al., 2018. 
- Finally, they show that lpNTK can be used to identify and prune easiest points to improve test accuracy, echoing findings from Paul et al., 2021 and Sorscher et al., 2022.

The experiments are conducted for a LeNet5/MNIST and ResNet18/CIFAR-10 setup due to limitations in computing the lpNTK.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths
===

1. A quantifications of intersample relationships can be a significantly useful tool and can be helpful for understanding a variety of concepts beyond what is covered in the paper.
2. The proposed quantity is (mostly) principled and followed naturally from the structure of gradient descent updates. The paper does makes some heuristic simplifications, which however make sense to me. The experimental results seem to suggest that these heuristic simplifications still preserve the significance of the quantity. The authors also show formally that the proposed lpNTK converges to the standard NTK asymptotically, which further alleviates concerns regarding the couple of heuristic jumps in the definition.
3. The paper covers a lot of ground, including connections to data pruning, forgeting events and learning difficulty. This validates the significance of the quantity. 
4. The authors do a great job building on various threads of existing work, and importantly, in giving due credit to them.
5. There are non-trivial technical challenges that the authors have tackled, such as how to define and identify redundant points using lpNTK, how to use lpNTK to group points etc.,


Weaknesses
===

It seemed to me that while there is a variety of experiments designed, each experiment in itself seems incomplete/not sufficiently substantiating the claims.

1. Sec 3.2 claims that _"the learning difficulty of samples is mainly due to
the interactions between them, rather than inherent properties of individual samples."_ This is a strong claim. The current argument  for this is that the learning difficulty of Jiang et al., 2021 and Ren et al., 2022 vary a lot as we increase the training set size. To better substantiate the claim, I'd expect to see:

- at the least that for various dataset sizes N, the inter-sample relationships of lpNTK consistently captures learning difficulty for that dataset size N. It's not clear if Experiment 3 actually verifies this for various values of N or just for one value of N. (may simply be a clarity issue)

 - Bonus: an experiment where one can intervene on the intersample relationships somehow (for a fixed dataset size), and show that learning difficulty correspondingly varies e.g., adding label noise, oversampling a particular subgroup etc., are some ways to vary intersample relationships. 


2. The analysis in Experiment 3 currently seems superficial to me. To show that learning difficulty is "correlated" with lpNTK-based clustering of points, the paper reports a single value, namely what % of the easiest samples fall in the largest cluster. There are many other natural visualizations here that would provide a more holistic picture: 

  - Where do the most difficult points fall? 
  - Conversely, what fraction of the largest cluster are very easy? 
  - And what fraction of the tail clusters are very hard? 
  - Can we plot the cluster size of a point on the x axis and its learning difficulty on y and see a correlation? 


3. A stronger paper would also have a way of showing why the proposed quantity (lpNTK) captures phenomena that other baseline quantities don't. Some candidate baselines include pNTK (which is evaluated only for the data pruning experiment) and the EL2N/GraND score. 
- It would have been valuable to show for example that the lpNTK is a better quantification of intersample relationships than other obvious/existing quantities, by showing that it can better capture forgetting events, example difficulty etc., Concretely, Table 1 misses a baseline to compare with.
- Alternatively, it would have been valuable to empirically show that quantities that don't look at intersample relationships are restrictive and capture only one phenomenon while lpNTK is able to unify multiple phenomena at the same time. 


Minor:
====
4. The paper could have explored results on CIFAR-100 instead of relatively more toy CIFAR-10, where ResNet-18 has reasonable accuracy.

5. I wonder if the paper would benefit from a better survey of the literature on influence functions  (which I'm not familiar with) besides the cited Koh and Liang, 2017.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The work is original, and builds off of and unifies multiple threads of existing work, which I view as a positive.


There are some minor clarity issues:
-  It's not clear if the proof of the theorem is mostly based off of Mohamadi & Sutherland (2022), or has non-trivial modifications. This didn't affect my score, but I think this is worth clarifying.
-  The paper uses "the above analysis" at multiple points, and it is not clear what it is referring to. e.g., In Sec 3.2, "Given our analysis above", is this referring to Sec 3.1? Again in Sec 3.4, "to verify the above analysis", unclear what analsysis.

Typo: "and note required for"  --> "and not required for"

The paper proposes a quantification of inter-sample relationships during training, which is mathematically well-motivated. The paper is also novel and broad in how it establishes connections between this quantity and various important concepts in deep learning. 
The experiments are however lacking and can be significantly improved in how they justify the stated claims.

As mentioned in the second last paragraph of Section 4.3, to prune the datasets, we randomly removed 10% of the samples in the largest cluster from FPC, which is heuristic as we discussed in Section 4.4. Since the core procedure is the clustering of samples, we provided the pseudocode of FPC with lpNTK in Appendix D.4 (of the updated version).

To decide the parameters for calculating lpNTK, we choose the $t$ which gives the best validation accuracy on held-out data, as briefly mentioned in the last paragraph on page 2. We’ll re-organise the structure in the future to make it more clear.

# Q3: Discussion on addressing the time complexity

```

In particular, the quadratic complexity makes it particularly difficult to scale. Discussion to address these problems could strengthen the paper.
```

Thanks for the suggestions. We’ll add discussion on possible improvements in the future.

# Q4: How is lpNTK fundamentally different from NTK

```
In general, I believe the community has established that NTK is not a particularly good formalism for understanding deep learning. Do you see lpNTK to be fundamentally different from NTK or does it inherit all the problems of NTK?
```

From our perspective, the way we derived lpNTK is actually different from NTK. We started from the first-order Taylor approximation to the *interactions* between samples, with a few assumptions. Unlike NTK, we did not try to capture the training dynamics of ANNs, but rather the relationships between samples. 

More importantly, NTK (not eNTK) assumes a “lazy regime” to make sure the kernel keeps constant over time. We, on the other hand, follow the empirical variant, thus do not need to rely on the lazy regime assumption.

```
Can you visualize what kind of data points a pruned? Are there any distinctive features or connections amongst the pruned data points?
```

Thanks for identifying these minor issues. We’ve solved the typo problem, and will add example samples in the future.

Thank you for identifying the clarity and appropriate experiment design of this work. We answer each of your concerns as follows.

# Q1: Lack of motivation for not using gradients

```
My main concern is lack of motivation for using this approximate analysis (based on the gradients of the output) instead of directly using the gradients of the loss at data points. Is there any reason that the authors did not use agreements between the gradients at different data points instead of directly looking at the direction of update resulting from a data point and the effect of this update on the loss at another data point? It seems to me that this is what the analysis in the submission tries to approximate but this quantity can be more accurately estimate by simply looking at the gradient of the loss at the two data points. See [1] as an example on the effect of agreement on the gradients on learning. I understand that this previous work is different from the submission. I'm only mentioning this as an example of working directly with gradients.
```

Similar to the prediction term we analysed in the last paragraph of Section 2.2, using agreements between the gradients is misleading. Suppose there are two identical samples in the training set and both are accurately predicted, i.e. $\hat{y}=y$, then both gradients are $0$. Thus, using agreements between the gradients as a similarity measure, we would get such a conclusion that the similarity between those two **identical** samples is $0$. Apparently, this doesn’t make sense. 

Approximating the interaction, on the other hand, allows us to decompose the effects from different parts of the model. More importantly, the first-order Taylor approximation connects the prediction changes with the SGD, as shown by the equation in the first paragraph of Appendix A. Without Taylor approximation, we need to calculate $||w^{t+1}-w^t||^n$ where $n\in\{1,2,\dots,\infty\}$, which is computationally intractable.

Lastly, we argue that our lpNTK similarity makes sense in practice. As shown in Section 4.2, even the model can accurately fit most of the training samples, many of them are still mostly similar to themselves under lpNTK, not like the gradient measure. We also checked that the lpNTK between well-learnt models are significantly greater than $0$.

# Q2: The choice of learning rate in Section 3.2 is unclear

```
The choice of learning rate has an important role in the results for Figure 1. Section 3.2 should state the strategy for choosing the learning rate.
```

In Section 3.2, we chose the learning rate $0.01$ to make sure that the model can converge on all datasets with varying sizes. We also ran the experiment on two extra learning rates, $0.1$ and $0.001$. The results are given in [https://ibb.co/0cbN42m](https://ibb.co/0cbN42m) and [https://ibb.co/Js6Lkk9](https://ibb.co/Js6Lkk9) respectively. As shown in both plots, the conclusion from Figure 1 still holds for varying learning rates. So, we argue that the learning rate is not a key premise for our conclusion.

# Q3: The procedure of predicting forgetting events in Section 3.3 is not stated

```
The procedure of predicting forgetting in Section 3.3 is not stated and it is hard to evaluate this section without knowing what predicting forgetting means.
```

We’ve added the details of Experiment 2 into Appendix D, see D.3 in the revised version. As mentioned in our overall response and withdrawal statement, we found that the description in our original description mismatched with our implementation. 

# Q4: Not practical as a data pruning strategy

```
Section 2.1 mentions that the model parameters that work well on the validation set are preferred for computing the proposed NTK. Does this mean that, in the data pruning experiment in Section 4, the model has to be first trained on the whole data to obtain these parameters and compute the NTK? If so, this method is not practical as a data pruning strategy.
```

Yes, we have to first train the model then de-bias the dataset. 

However, the overall aim of this work is not to propose a data pruning strategy. We focus on the interactions between samples during learning, and how we can understand the learning of models on a given dataset and utilise them in order to improve the generalisation performance. The data de-biasing experiment is a specific use case to support the effectiveness of our lpNTK.

More importantly, as mentioned in the last paragraph of Section 5, a major difference between this work and data pruning is that “we aim to show that it is possible to *improve* the generalisation performance via removing samples”

# Minor Issues:

```
Kappa at the end of section 2.1 is undefined.
```

We’ve updated the main body and changed the $\kappa$ with “scalar”.

content.title: Overall response
content.comment:
We want to thank the reviewers for their time, constructive feedback, and diligent reviews. Please find responses to your comments and questions below. We have made updates to the paper, which are summarized below in a list of Major Updates and then described in detail how the updates address the reviewers’ comments.

We summarise the Major Updates to the paper as follows:

1. We replaced “lpNTK” with “eNTK” in Section 3.3 and Appendix D.3 (newly added) since we spotted a mistake we made in our implementation. More details about this mistake are illustrated in our Withdrawal Statement
2. We added a new appendix section (Appendix D.2) to clearly describe how we ran the learning difficulty experiments as discussed in Section 3.2.
3. We added a new appendix section (Appendix D.3) to outline the experiments on predicting forgetting events. At this moment, we keep the “eNTK” rather than using “lpNTK” to match with our implementation.
4. We corrected the typos and other minor issues identified by the reviewers.

content.title: Withdrawal Statement
content.comment:
Dear AC and reviewers:

We appreciate the comments, suggestions, and feedback from you thus far. They have helped us to improve the quality and soundness of this submission. We also appreciate the reviewers for identifying the novelty and potential contribution of this work to the community.

However, during the formalisation of Experiment 3 in our submission, we spotted a problem in our implementation. We found that our implementation of lpNTK in Section 3.3 was actually mathematically equivalent to eNTK, thus the results shown in Table 1 are inaccurate. Though this error hasn’t occurred in other places, to guarantee the soundness and reliability of our findings, we decided to withdraw this submission. 

In the revised version, we have replaced all “lpNTK” in Section 3.3 with “eNTK” and struck across “lpNTK” to highlight the change. In fact, the problem could be fixed with a few updates to the implementation. But, one of our authors is now having some family issue to deal with thus was not able to fix the problem in time.

Based on the feedback we received, we see great potential of our method and believe that we can improve this work even further. We hope to provide deeper insights about various learning phenomena we discussed in Section 3 and contribute a more substantial tool in the future.

To sum up, we would like to withdraw the current submission, and take this as a chance to further improve the quality and contribution of this work. Thank you again for your time and the great feedback!

Best regards,

Authors of submission 2828

content.title: Thanks
content.comment:
Dear authors,

Thanks for your transparency and integrity --- it is natural for mistakes like these to happen, but what matters is how you respond to it. Glad you found our feedback useful. Good luck with updating the paper and submitting it to a future conference. 
And I sincerely hope that the author's personal issues are resolved soon!
